slides.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce service in 2027?
Key questions

claims.claim: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service, in 2027 while reaching profit within its $12.0M of cash and keeping 12 months of runway?
evidence: Decision maker: The board (two founders and two investors)

Success criteria: A path to profitability within the current $12.0M of cash, with no new funding round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; Contribution profit per order by month 18, as the founders' model claims
Timing: Board meeting, January 2027
Out of scope: Cities beyond the three planned; A new funding round; The software product roadmap

Sub-questions: 1 Is quick commerce a market in which a new regional entrant can make money? 2 Can Parcelbird Now make money on each order once store costs are counted? 3 Did Columbus show the density and loyalty the model needs, at an affordable cost? 4 Can the launch be funded with 12 months of runway, and is there a better use of the cash? 5 What should Parcelbird do in 2027, and when would it revisit an own service?

slides.title: Executive summary

claims.claim: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: orders lose money on all the evidence and the plan breaks the runway floor; grow the software business instead
Quick commerce is growing fast, but neither incumbent has found a way to make money from it
evidence: QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; grow the software business instead. Decide against the launch in January, fund four software hires and sell store-based fast delivery to grocers. Reopen the question only when customer sites pass four tests.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Do not launch: none on evidence (every observed set of inputs loses money per order); fails runway test with about six months left at month 18, even on the plan's own numbers
Recommended: break-even at about $11M of ARR, about two years out at 60% growth; profit within the cash and no capex, if hiring follows signed deals

alternatives_considered.option: Copy Zipcart's fee and promotion fix
alternatives_considered.treatment: Would still leave the median store about $1 short on every order (−$1.05) once volume falls 14%

alternatives_considered.option: Sell store-based fast delivery to grocers (supplier rather than competitor)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen as step 3: be the supplier of fast delivery to grocers rather than their competitor; no $5.4M dark-store capex

Left out as out of scope: the plan names Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City

assumptions_and_uncertainties: The briefing pack holds no city-level data on rivals in Columbus, Indianapolis or Kansas City; "nobody owns the Midwest" is not tested
Incumbents' contribution per order is not defined in the pack, so it is compared with Parcelbird's figures only loosely
Per-order loss excludes head office and launch marketing, so losses are understated
Best observed inputs combine best order value and best density from different sites; no site had both
Zipcart fix analysis assumes the fee carries no extra payment cost and riders keep 2.4 orders an hour at lower volume
Rider pay held at $17.75 an hour; size of any minimum pay standard is not yet known; affected cities not named
A permanent store might do better than the temporary pop-up, but nothing in the pack shows by how much
Survey and pop-up cover different groups, so the gap is intent against use rather than like-for-like
Payback assumes no churn after month three and excludes first two months of orders; store fixed costs not charged to the customer, which flatters the result
Acquisition estimate assumes Columbus behavior holds in all three cities, every customer won at $38, word of mouth not counted
The pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes the current $0.4M monthly burn; the deck uses the kinder reading
Pipeline win rates are not in the pack, so the full pipeline bar is an upper bound
Software path assumes costs flat apart from $0.8M of hires, 81% gross margin and 60% ARR growth; at 30% growth cash ends 2028 under the floor (~$2.95M, about 10.5 months)
Biggest risk: the software path rests on 60% growth holding
Rider-pay sensitivity steps of $1 an hour are a team choice for illustration
